uncited: Multi-Resolution and Level of Detail (LOD) techniques optimize volume and point cloud rendering by decomposing data into hierarchical structures, allowing the renderer to select primitives of varying granularity based on spatial error or screen-space footprint .

This family solves the performance bottleneck of rendering high-density data by replacing clusters of fine primitives with single, aggregated coarse primitives in homogeneous or distant regions, while preserving detail in complex or foreground areas .

It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by its reliance on explicit error metrics or fixed downsampling rates to drive the selection of the appropriate resolution level, rather than relying solely on static distance thresholds or fixed grid subdivisions .
The methods in this family share the mechanism of hierarchical decomposition and error-driven or distance-driven primitive selection, building on [Splatting](23-splatting.md) .
Hierarchical Decomposition: The input data is organized into a tree structure (e.g., octree, pyramid, or sequential point tree) .
Each node represents a spatial region and stores aggregate properties (mean position, average color/density, total opacity, or merged covariance) derived from its children .
Error Metric Computation: For each internal node, a local error metric $E$ is computed to quantify the approximation cost of representing the node's children with the node's aggregate properties .
Common metrics include the Root Mean Square (RMS) error of scalar values or the deviation of child positions/opacities from the parent's mean .
Adaptive Traversal and Selection: During rendering, the hierarchy is traversed from the root to the leaves.

A node is selected as a leaf (and thus rendered as a single primitive) if its error $E$ is below a user-defined threshold $\epsilon$ or if its projected screen-space footprint is smaller than a pixel threshold .
If the error exceeds the threshold, the algorithm recurses to the children .
Primitive Aggregation: When a node is selected, its children are merged into a single representative primitive.
The primitive's attributes are computed as weighted averages or sums of the children's attributes .
For Gaussian splats, this involves merging covariances and spherical harmonics coefficients .

Multi-Resolution Rendering: The final image is composed of primitives from various levels of the hierarchy, allowing for efficient culling of distant or homogeneous regions while maintaining fidelity in foreground or complex areas .
Early work by Laur and Hanrahan (1991) introduced hierarchical point clouds using error metrics .

Subsequent developments extended these ideas to volumetric splatting using pyramidal structures  and more recently to 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle the memory constraints of neural radiance fields .
